name: Mobile Product
tagline: One app on both platforms, usable offline, with a server-side switch for when a build is wrong
summary: A stack for a consumer or business app on iOS and Android. Every choice here follows from three constraints the web does not have: the network fails mid-request, the OS can suspend you, and you cannot hotfix a shipped binary.
basis: TechFlow archetype, not a specific company's stack. It reflects the defaults we would pick for a product team shipping both platforms with a small mobile group and an existing backend.

items.note: One codebase and real platform views when the team already writes React.
Native where platform capability or interface fidelity is the product.
The Android half of the same decision.
Read this before committing — the choice is architectural, not a feature comparison.
The screen renders from local rows; the network only updates them.
Not a feature. It is what stops a lift from emptying the app.
Apply the write locally, reconcile later — the only way a tap feels instant on cellular.
Short timeouts, batched requests, transfers handed to the OS.
Every write carries a key, because a retry is unavoidable and a double charge is not.
Backoff with jitter, so a tower blip does not become a thundering herd.
Delta sync, presigned uploads, push fan-out and a version gate.
One place for TLS, token checks, rate limits and the app-version header.
Two-year-old builds are still in production traffic. Plan for it or break them.
Sign-in in the system browser; refresh token in the platform keystore.
Short-lived access tokens, revocable refresh — never a long-lived token in app storage.
Direct upload with a presigned URL so large files never pass through the API.
Images dominate mobile bytes; serve them from an edge and keep egress off the origin.
A pointer, not a payload — delivery is best effort and lands on a lock screen.
The queue and worker behind it, so a gateway outage is a backlog.
Someone else approves the build; plan the cadence around it.
Ship dark, release with a switch. The only recovery path for a bad binary.
Signing, screenshots and upload automated — manual release engineering rots.

items.label: Crash reporting per app version
items.note: Crash-free rate of the *new* version, not the average across all of them.
Client-side request timing segmented by connection type — p95 on cellular is the real number.

whenToUse: The product needs to be usable with no connection, or on a bad one
You ship to both iOS and Android and want one team to maintain it
The app writes data, so retries and conflicts are real rather than theoretical
Release cadence matters and you cannot afford a review cycle per fix
tradeoffs: Offline sync is the most expensive part of a mobile product, and there is no cheap version
Every feature flag is a code path that stays in the binary and eventually needs removing
Cross-platform saves implementation time and spends it on per-platform polish and native dependencies
Supporting old app versions constrains every API you ship, for years
A local database means schema migrations on devices you do not control
